KEY MESSAGE 1 DESCRIPTION...

Showers and thunderstorms are underway across much of New
Hampshire this afternoon as a moist airmass moves into daytime
instability.

The environment has a number of components supporting heavy
rainfall rates through early evening: high PWATs, low steering
flow, and ample instability. PWAT values around 1.5 to 2" are
being supporting by southerly vapor transport ahead of closed
low exiting the Great Lakes. The broad nature of the low lacks
a strong LLJ at this time, thus low shear and storm motion is 
expected. This overlap with daytime instability and generous
dewpoint temps means showers and storms will continue to develop
and wash out into early evening.

The primary threat with these storms will be lightning and heavy
downpours, where repetitive training or slow storm motion could
result in isolated flash flooding. Urban areas will also be
susceptible due to poor drainage should these heavy storms roll
through. Rain rates at area weather stations have generally 
been 2 to 4 inches per hour. This is expected given the 
environment. The good news is the lack of shear has allowed most
storms to rain into their updrafts, reducing their longevity. 
Thus while these rates are concerning, they haven't been 
sustained long enough to overcome otherwise high flash flood 
guidance in the region. Will continue to monitor the area 
through early evening, as repeat rounds of heavy rainfall over 
recently saturated ground will tend to increase this threat.

The large, dynamic system in the region will slowly pivot 
eastward overnight. Guidance today has ramped up QPF in New 
England overnight, with a pivoting band of forced rainfall 
occurs just west of New Hampshire overnight. This will slowly
near western New Hampshire through the early morning hours
Wednesday. Across the rest of the forecast area, onshore flow
increases and will continue to advect moisture inland. It is
expected that stratus will fill in, with fog developing along
the coast and interior overnight.

KEY MESSAGE 2 DESCRIPTION...

Cutoff low pressure will move across the Delmarva on Wednesday 
morning to southern New England on Thursday before slowly exiting to 
the east over the Gulf of Maine by Friday. This will continue to 
bring periods of moderate to locally heavy rainfall to the region 
with the most impactful period expected to be on Wednesday. 
Temperatures will generally be below avg through the end of the week 
given the onshore flow combined with clouds and rainfall. 

The H85 SE LLJ will increase during the day on Wednesday, which may 
allow for some backbuilding of convective showers within an expected 
favorable environment for heavy rainfall. The latest 12Z HREF 
ensemble mean 24-hr QPF through 00Z Thursday ranges from between 1-
2" across much of south-central NH with less than an inch elsewhere. 
Portions of northwestern ME may mot see much rainfall during the 
day. As a result, an isolated to scattered flash flood threat 
exists, especially where cells do manage to back build and fall
across both the urban corridors and the mountainous terrain of 
NH. River flooding is unlikely given the large available storage
space but rises on rivers and streams can be expected. High 
temperatures will be mainly into the 70s but high dew points 
will make it quite muggy. 

Periods of showers and embedded downpours will continue on 
Thursday, with the highest rainfall amounts expected across 
south-central NH and extending into southwestern ME. The showers
will be very slow moving with backbuilding possible, and 
therefore a flash flood threat will remain... especially given 
that soils will likely be already saturated in some locations. 
Flow will become more northeasterly on Thursday night, with a 
diminishing flash flood threat. 

Total rainfall is currently expected to range from less than an inch 
across northwestern ME and into northern Coos county NH with 
generally between 1-3" of rain further to the south. The 12Z HREF 
LPMM does show the potential for localized amounts of up to around 
5", with the areas of greatest concern for these amounts across the 
Whites as well as across southern NH. 

The cutoff low will finally exit to our east on Fri, allowing 
for brightening skies and high temperatures of around 80 
degrees. 

KEY MESSAGE 3 DESCRIPTION...

Saturday should feature drier conditions as the cutoff low 
dissipates over the Gulf of ME. Highs will be into the lower 80s 
with partly cloudy skies. Sunday into early next week looks to be 
potentially unsettled again at times as a series of disturbances 
cross down from the north, allowing for scattered showers and 
storms. This will help to keep temperatures near seasonable avg
with no significant heat in sight as we head into the month of 
August.
